Type here to try the keyboard
Hold and slide left or right on the space bar

Phayz Keyboard brings the Windows Phone keyboard to Android: flat keys and big light type. This short tour shows what it can do. You can open it again from the three dots in the keyboard (the ? button) or from the settings.

Tap the arrow for a capital; tap it twice (or hold it) to lock capitals. \"?123\" switches to numbers and symbols, and \"=\<\" to more of them. The smiley opens emoji and the globe changes language (hide the globe in the settings to widen the space bar; then hold the space bar to change language). Press Enter for the action of the field (search, send, next…).

Hold a key and a bar appears above it with accents, digits and symbols. Slide your finger to one of them and let go. If you let go without sliding, you get the first one, the accented letter; the plain letter is in the bar. How long to hold is in Settings → Typing (200 ms to start).

Put your finger on the first letter of a word and slide over the others without lifting. The word appears with a space. If it is not the one you wanted, tap another in the bar above the keys. Works in the language you are using.
Slide your finger left or right on the space bar to move the cursor through the text, one character at a time. Two quick spaces type a full stop and a space.

Three words appear above the keys while you type; the one in colour is what space will insert. Typos are fixed when you end a word, and if the fix is wrong, Backspace right away gives back what you typed. After a word, the likely next word is offered, and sometimes a whole phrase marked with \"…\". Offensive words are never suggested. Everything is learned on this phone only.
The three dots and the quick button

The three dots on the left of the bar open the toolbox: clipboard, emoji, voice, help and settings. The button on the right goes straight to one tool, the clipboard by default, and shows a dot when you have just copied something. Choose which tool it opens in Settings → Typing.

Everything you copy is kept, on this phone only. Tap an item to paste it, the pin to keep it for good, the cross to delete it. Copied photos are kept too and are pasted as pictures where the app allows it. You choose how many items are kept in Settings → Clipboard.

Type a colon and a word, like :dog, and the matching emoji appear in the suggestion bar: slide them sideways and tap one to replace what you typed. In the emoji panel, the magnifier searches by name with the keyboard itself. The names are in your language and in English. Smart emoji search can be switched off in Settings → Suggestions.

The smiley key opens emoji by category, with the recent ones first. Hold a hand or a person for skin tones. The last two tabs hold the classic emoticons, :-) and friends, and the Japanese kaomoji, which work in every app.

Tap the microphone in the toolbox and speak: the words appear as you talk. With \"Keep listening\" on (Settings → Voice) it keeps transcribing until you tap the microphone again. The first time Android asks to allow the microphone.

Five looks: Classic (flat Windows Phone), Modern Glass, Modern Droid, iPhone and Modern Slate, each dark, light or following the system. Pick one colour of your own (Modern Droid follows your wallpaper), or use a photo behind the keys: its brightest colour becomes your colour. \"Colour follows the app\" can also tint the keyboard like the app under it (it needs an accessibility service that reads no text).

In Settings → Size and layout you can make the keys taller or shorter (separately in landscape), make the keyboard narrower and put it on the left or right for one-handed use, change the space between keys, and show a number row.

Turn on the languages you write in (Settings → Languages) and switch with the globe key. Seventeen layouts are included; you can import any other layout, and a full dictionary for any language, to get better corrections and predictions.

No trackers, no analytics. What you type, what the keyboard learns and your clipboard stay on this phone and are left out of backups. Nothing is learned in password fields. The internet is used only to look for a new version of the keyboard, and the microphone only for voice typing. You can export or erase what was learned in Settings → Suggestions.

Turn the keyboard on, step by step
Let\'s turn your new keyboard on. It takes a minute, and each step notices by itself when it is done.
Open the list of keyboards and switch on Phayz Keyboard. Android shows a standard warning about all keyboards; this one keeps everything on your phone and sends nothing anywhere.
Now pick Phayz Keyboard as the keyboard you type with.
To dictate, the keyboard needs the microphone. You can skip this and allow it later.
Type something here. Try holding a letter, sliding over the space bar, and tapping the three dots.
The keyboard is ready. Want a short tour of what it can do? You can find it again anytime in the settings.

That is not a backup of Phayz Keyboard

Settings → Size and layout → Automatic calibration. Type a few sentences and the keyboard measures where your fingers land. It corrects your touches without moving the keys, learns the curve of your thumb, and grows the keys if you still miss. The fixes are put to work between one sentence and the next, so you see the keyboard improve. Nothing is kept until you tap Apply, and nothing leaves your phone.

The keyboard does not only look for the nearest word: it weighs where your finger landed (a tap between two keys makes either one likely), the word you wrote before, how common each word is and which corrections you undid. When two fixes are equally likely it shows both and changes nothing. It also offers a missing space ("thankyou" → "thank you"). All of this runs on the phone and learns only from what you type; switch it off in Settings → Suggestions.

In Settings → Backup and restore you can save everything the app keeps in one file: settings, learned words, imported dictionaries and layouts, the clipboard and your picture. Restore it on another phone, or after installing the app again with another signature. The file holds your keys and what you typed, so keep it private.

Looks only at github.com/%1$s. The request carries no identifier of you or your phone. Android checks that the new version is signed with the same key as this one before it installs it.
Version %1$s. Tap to see what is new.

Every 12 hours the keyboard looks in its own repository on GitHub, and only there, for a new version. When there is one, a blue tile appears at the top of Start; Settings → Updates shows what is new and downloads and installs it. Android only installs it if it is signed with the same key as the one you have. You can switch the check off, or press Check now.
